title: Management of Female Genital Mutilation Complications

headings.title: Introduction and Overview of Female Genital Mutilation
headings.content: Female Genital Mutilation (FGM), also known as female genital cutting, comprises all procedures that involve partial or total removal of the external female genitalia or other injury to the female genital organs for non-medical reasons. Recognized globally as a violation of the human rights of girls and women, FGM is deeply rooted in cultural, religious, and social myths that attempt to control female sexuality, ensure chastity, or promote hygiene and aesthetic ideals. In Nigeria, the practice varies significantly across different ethnic groups and geographic zones, with high prevalence rates particularly documented in the southern and southwestern regions, though practiced nationwide. As nursing students and future healthcare professionals in Nigeria, understanding FGM is essential because affected women frequently present to clinical settings with a myriad of physical, obstetric, psychological, and urological complications. Healthcare providers must approach FGM with cultural sensitivity while remaining steadfast in their commitment to patient-centered care and eradication. Recognizing the different types of FGM—ranging from type I (clitoridectomy) to type III (infibulation, or the narrowing of the vaginal orifice with creation of a covering seal)—allows nurses to anticipate specific clinical challenges. Comprehensive care requires not only treating acute injuries or chronic physical pain but also addressing the profound emotional and psychosexual trauma endured by survivors. Through dedicated education, advocacy, and clinical competence, Nigerian nurses play a vital frontline role in mitigating the devastating consequences of FGM and supporting affected communities toward total abandonment of the practice.

headings.title: Immediate and Long-Term Complications of FGM
headings.content: The complications of Female Genital Mutilation are extensive and can be categorized into immediate and long-term effects, profoundly impacting a woman's physical, psychological, and reproductive health. Immediate complications often occur at the time of the procedure, which is traditionally performed under unsterile conditions by traditional practitioners without anesthesia. These acute issues include severe hemorrhage, intense pain, shock, acute urine retention due to swelling or injury, local infections such as tetanus and sepsis, and damage to adjacent anatomical structures like the urethra, vagina, perineum, and rectum. Long-term complications develop gradually and persist over a lifetime, affecting daily comfort and reproductive health. Chronic pain during menstruation, recurring urinary tract infections (UTIs) resulting from anatomical obstruction, dyspareunia (painful sexual intercourse), and chronic pelvic inflammatory disease are exceptionally common. Furthermore, women with type III FGM (infibulation) frequently experience haematocolpos, where menstrual blood is trapped behind the scar tissue seal, leading to cyclical lower abdominal pain and hematuria. Obstetric complications are also severe, manifesting as prolonged labor, obstructed labor, perineal tears, obstetric fistula, and increased rates of neonatal morbidity and perinatal mortality. For Nigerian nurses, identifying these symptoms early is crucial for providing targeted therapeutic interventions and holistic nursing management that addresses both physical ailments and emotional scars.

headings.title: Initial Clinical Assessment and History Taking
headings.content: Initial clinical assessment and comprehensive history taking for women presenting with a history of FGM require a high degree of empathy, confidentiality, and professional skill. Many survivors carry deep trauma and shame, making it vital for nurses and midwives to establish a safe, non-judgmental environment. The assessment begins with a thorough history that explores the patient's cultural background, the type of FGM performed if known, the age at which it occurred, and specific symptoms such as chronic pain, urinary difficulties, or sexual dysfunction. Physical examination must be performed with extreme gentleness, ensuring informed consent is obtained at every step, and explaining clearly what the examination entails. The nurse should document the anatomical findings meticulously, noting the degree of scarring, presence of labial fusion, patency of the vaginal introitus, and signs of chronic infection or obstruction. It is also important to assess psychological well-being, screening for symptoms of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), anxiety, and depression. A sensitive approach helps build rapport, allowing the patient to articulate her health needs and goals, whether she is seeking relief from physical pain, preparing for marriage or childbirth, or requesting surgical defibulation. Effective history taking bridges the gap between clinical intervention and compassionate nursing care, ensuring that the patient feels empowered and respected throughout her healthcare journey.

headings.title: Surgical Management: Defibulation and Reconstruction
headings.content: Surgical management for women with FGM complications primarily involves defibulation (also known deroofing or opening) and, in some cases, reconstructive procedures. Defibulation is a surgical procedure that cuts open the scar tissue seal created during infibulation (Type III FGM) to restore normal anatomical access to the vagina, urethra, and clitoris. This procedure is frequently indicated for women suffering from obstructed menses (haematocolpos), recurrent urinary tract infections, inability to engage in penetrative intercourse, or preparation for safe childbirth. Defibulation can be performed under local or regional anesthesia, where the fused scar tissue is carefully incised along the midline, and the edges are sutured to prevent re-fusion. Post-operative care requires meticulous wound hygiene, pain management, and pelvic floor exercises to maintain vaginal patency and promote healing. While clitoral reconstruction is sometimes requested by survivors to restore external genital appearance or partial sensation, it is a specialized surgical intervention that requires careful patient counseling regarding realistic expectations, potential risks, and the availability of trained surgical specialists. Nurses play a crucial role in preparing the patient pre-operatively, assisting during the procedure, providing empathetic post-operative wound care, and educating the patient on maintaining hygiene and managing recovery at home.

headings.title: Psychological and Psychosexual Support
headings.content: The psychological and psychosexual impact of FGM is profound, often leaving survivors with lifelong emotional burdens, anxiety, and sexual dysfunction. Because the procedure involves violation of a young girl's bodily integrity, often accompanied by severe trauma and betrayal by trusted caregivers, survivors frequently experience post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), chronic anxiety, depression, and low self-esteem. Psychosexually, women may suffer from severe dyspareunia, lack of sexual desire, anorgasmia, and fear associated with sexual intimacy due to physical pain and scar tissue constriction. Comprehensive management mandates integrated psychological support, including trauma-informed counseling, cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT), and sex therapy when appropriate. Nurses must provide a compassionate, empathetic listening ear, validating the patient's emotional pain without judgment. It is also important to involve partners in counseling sessions where culturally appropriate and consented to, as partner understanding and patience are vital for overcoming psychosexual challenges and rebuilding intimacy. By normalizing these discussions and offering referrals to specialized mental health professionals, nurses help survivors reclaim their bodily autonomy, heal from emotional trauma, and improve their overall quality of life.

headings.title: Obstetric and Gynecological Care for Affected Women
headings.content: Obstetric and gynecological care for women affected by FGM requires specialized clinical knowledge to ensure safe pregnancies, deliveries, and management of reproductive health issues. During antenatal care, midwives and nurses must conduct early pelvic assessments to determine if defibulation is required before or during labor. Infibulated women are at high risk for obstructed labor, prolonged second stage of labor, severe perineal lacerations, and fetal distress due to the inelastic scar tissue acting as a mechanical barrier. If defibulation has not been performed prior to pregnancy, it must be performed antenatally or as an emergency procedure at the time of delivery (anterior incision) to allow safe passage of the fetus and prevent extensive tearing. Following delivery, prompt and precise repair of episiotomies or lacerations is crucial, avoiding re-infibulation, as re-infibulation violates human rights and medical ethics. Gynecologically, care includes managing chronic pelvic pain, treating recurring urinary tract infections, clearing haematocolpos, and providing family planning counseling tailored to the patient's anatomical realities and preferences. Nigerian nurses and midwives must advocate for evidence-based obstetric practices that prioritize maternal and neonatal safety while respecting the emotional and physical vulnerabilities of FGM survivors.

headings.title: Nursing Interventions and Patient Advocacy
headings.content: Nursing interventions and patient advocacy are central to mitigating the impacts of FGM and supporting affected women through comprehensive healthcare delivery. Nurses act as direct care providers, educators, counselors, and advocates within hospitals, primary healthcare clinics, and community health outreaches across Nigeria. Clinical nursing interventions include meticulous wound care, pain management, administering prescribed antibiotics, monitoring vital signs, and offering compassionate emotional support. Beyond the bedside, nurses advocate for patients by ensuring that healthcare environments remain culturally safe, confidential, and free from stigma or judgment from healthcare personnel. Patient education is another vital pillar; nurses must educate women and girls about reproductive anatomy, hygiene practices, and their legal rights regarding bodily autonomy. Furthermore, nurses must advocate for policy changes within healthcare institutions to ensure standardized protocols for managing FGM complications, including training staff on defibulation and trauma-informed care. By standing up for the rights of survivors and providing uncompromising, empathetic care, Nigerian nurses contribute significantly to both individual healing and the broader societal movement to end the practice of FGM.

headings.title: Prevention, Legal Frameworks, and Community Education in Nigeria
headings.content: Prevention, legal frameworks, and community education are essential pillars in the ultimate eradication of Female Genital Mutilation in Nigeria. At the national level, the Violence Against Persons (Prohibition) (VAPP) Act, signed into law in 2015, provides a comprehensive legal framework prohibiting FGM and prescribing penalties for offenders, alongside various state-level edicts and child rights laws. However, legislation alone is insufficient without active community engagement, grassroots sensitization, and behavioral change communication. Healthcare professionals, particularly nurses and community health extension workers, are uniquely positioned to lead community education programs. These programs target traditional rulers, religious leaders, parents, youth groups, and traditional circumcisers, debunking myths surrounding hygiene, fertility, and morality linked to FGM. Community-led initiatives that provide alternative sources of income for traditional practitioners who rely on FGM for livelihood have also proven successful. Nurses must participate in advocacy campaigns, collaborate with non-governmental organizations (NGOs), and integrate FGM education into antenatal and school health programs. Through sustained educational efforts, legal enforcement, and compassionate community dialogue, Nigeria can foster a cultural shift toward protecting the girl child and abandoning FGM permanently.
